Introduce price tiers for micro pharmacies The impact we observed* Conclusion: what this taught me as a product manager Product Management Pharmacy Point Of Sale Product Strategy Product Acquisition Challenge: How a Pharmacist Helped Micro Pharmacies Run Better Through an App Patricia S 8 min read · Just now -- Listen Share Why pharmacies weren’t buying our point-of-sale system, and how two tested hypotheses turned into three product decisions. Before I became a product manager, I trained and was licensed as a pharmacist. So when I joined a pharmaceutical distributor in Indonesia to work on a cloud point-of-sale system for independent pharmacies, I already knew the daily reality of our users: serving patients at the counter, keeping stock of thousands of items, ordering from distributors, and keeping records that regulators can check. Our POS system covered all of that in one app: a cashier, purchasing, inventory, finance reports, and stock synced with online marketplaces. The product was solid. The problem was that not enough pharmacies were buying it. This is how I worked out why, and what we changed. Step 1: Size the market and see where we stand The first step was to understand how much room we had to grow. Indonesia had roughly 30,000 pharmacies in 2024, and most of them were small, independent businesses rather than chains. Roughly 80% were ‘mom-and-pop’ neighbourhood pharmacies, micro enterprise, 10% were independent multi-branch local pharmacies (medium enterprise), and the rest 10% were Corporate-owned pharmacy chains (Source: GP Pharmacy Indonesia). A 2022 survey we ran with 1,255 pharmacies showed how much of this market was still untouched: 651 of them (52%) had no point-of-sale system at all. They were still running on paper, spreadsheets or memory. Against that, our POS had acquired about 2,400 pharmacies, roughly 8% of the market. The opportunity was huge. The question was why we were capturing so little of it. Step 2: Map the funnel and find the biggest drop Next, to identify the problem in the process, I mapped the acquisition funnel from first sales visit to real daily use: Press enter or click to view image in full size The biggest leak was right at the top. More than 8 in 10 pharmacies we visited didn’t buy. Once a pharmacy bought, most of them went live. That gave me one clear question: why wouldn’t pharmacies buy our package? I narrowed it to two possible answers: Our unique selling point wasn’t convincing, or Our price was too high. Step 3: Validate Hypothesis Hypothesis 1: a weak selling point Our POS was pitched on two main promises: Sell online: connect the pharmacy to marketplaces and reach new customers. Run operations and grow offline sales: manage the counter, stock and purchasing in one system. If pharmacies weren’t convinced, I needed to know which promise actually mattered to them. So I looked at what our existing customers really did in the app. I segmented 930 merchants by their share of online transactions and their monthly online sales: Press enter or click to view image in full size That means 91.6% of our merchants used Our POS mainly for in-store operations , and by sales value offline outweighed online by about 8 to 1. Our 2022 survey pointed the same way: only about 4,600 pharmacies said they were interested in selling online, against 8,900 that were not. Verdict: selling online is a real benefit, but only for a small group. Most pharmacies buy a POS to run their operations and grow sales at the counter. So, focusing only on selling online would be a misdirection. Hypothesis 2: inconvenient pricing Press enter or click to view image in full size At first glance, retention looked healthy. Monthly active users (MAU) grew steadily from October 2023 to June 2024, up 39%. But the total was hiding something. Monthly net growth shrank from +53 in December 2023 to just +12 in June 2024. New users kept arriving at a steady 36–71 a month. What changed was losses: pharmacies that were active one month and gone the next rose from 10 to between 33 and 44 a month. When I broke those losses down by pharmacy size, the answer was clear: Micro pharmacies made up about 9 in 10 lost users. Under Indonesian regulation, a micro business can have sales of up to Rp 2 billion a year, but most of the micro pharmacies we served sold a small fraction of that. After paying for medicines, rent and a pharmacist’s salary, a fixed Rp 350,000 subscription was a real burden, especially for new pharmacies whose income wasn’t stable yet. The pharmacies that most needed a system, small ones with no POS, were exactly the ones that found the full price hardest to justify. Verdict: price was a real barrier for micro pharmacies. And since small pharmacies make up a large part of the untouched market, the same price was likely stopping many of them from buying in the first place. Step 4: Three decisions to support offline sales Both findings pointed the same way: pharmacies valued Our POS as a tool to run their store and sell more at the counter, and smaller ones needed a price that matched their size. I focused on three moves. 1. Add value that grows the pharmacy’s sales We partnered with pharmaceutical principals (drug manufacturers) on online-to-offline campaigns that drove demand to POS for pharmacies. This gave pharmacies a concrete reason to join: being on the system could bring them more sales, not just better records.
